title: On the Intrinsic Limits of Transformer Image Embeddings in Non-Solvable Spatial Reasoning
claim: Models fail simple compositional transformation tasks because a constant-depth encoder cannot preserve group structure in latent space, so real embeddings drift from expected ones.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; chat failure example then encoder-to-latent diagram with expected vs real trajectories
description: Two framed panels. The left, with a red border and pink background, shows a chat between a user avatar and a generative model, marked by a blue star icon. The user asks for a rabbit, then for a rotation along the X-axis, then for a rotation back along the X-axis. The final bubble shows a rabbit that does not match the original, flagged with a red not-equal sign. The right panel has a green border. It shows a column of rabbit renders linked by arrows labelled RotX, RotY, RotY and RotZ (g1, g2, g3). The images feed a stack of green encoder slabs labelled 'Constant-depth Encoder'. Dashed lines lead to a latent-space column. A straight green dashed line marks the expected trajectory. A curved red dashed line marks the real trajectory, which drifts away. A boxed inset shows 'g_i ∈ G', 'G ≅ H?' and 'ρ(g_i) ∈ H'. The eye goes first to the red-versus-green contrast.
caption: From Empirical Spatial Failures to the Homomorphism Alignment Problem. (Left) The Spatial Reasoning Problem: Evidence of foundation models failing simple mental rotation tasks. (Right) The Homomorphism Alignment Problem: Can a constantdepth encoder map observations transformed by group G to a latent space where induced dynamics H are isomorphic to G (H ∼= G)? The analysis demonstrates that for non-solvable groups, this isomorphism is prohibited by architectural complexity constraints.
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) excel in semantic recognition but exhibit systematic failures in spatial reasoning tasks such as mental rotation. While often attributed to data scale, this work argues that the limitation arises from the intrinsic circuit complexity of the architecture. By formalizing spatial understanding as learning a Group Homomorphism Problem -- where latent embeddings preserve the algebraic structure of physical transformations acting on images -- we identify a fundamental computational bottleneck. Specifically, for non-solvable groups (e.g., $\mathrm{SO}(3)$), maintaining such structure-preserving embeddings is lowerbounded by the Word Problem, which is $\mathsf{NC^1}$-complete. In contrast, constant-depth ViTs with polynomial precision are strictly bounded by the complexity class $\mathsf{TC^0}$. Under the standard conjecture $\mathsf{TC^0} \subsetneq \mathsf{NC^1}$, a complexity boundary emerges: constant-depth architectures lack the logical depth required to capture non-solvable spatial structures in a single forward pass. To empirically validate this theoretical gap, we propose the Latent Space Algebra (LSA) benchmark, which reveals a significant degradation in ViT representations as the compositional depth of non-solvable tasks increases.
